publications.title: Modelling of Traffic Collisions at Road Intersections in Cape Town, South Africa: A Bayesian Spatio-Temporal Approach
publications.abstract: Abstract This paper models road traffic collision counts recorded between 2015 and 2019 in a ward located in the central part of Cape Town in South Africa, using a Bayesian spatio-temporal zero-inflated Negative Binomial approach. The method accounted for the excess zeros present in collision data by separately modeling zero and non-zero collision counts, while also capturing spatial and temporal dependencies through prior distributions. Road-level information was used as fixed-effects covariates, including speed limits, presence of traffic calming measures, traffic signals, road class, number of lanes, whether the intersection is on “Main Road”, and whether a public transport route passes through the intersection. The results reveal that among the covariates included in the selected model, node degree (used as a proxy for traffic flow), the presence of traffic signals, having any major road around the intersection (road class), location along “Main Road”, and the presence of a taxi route at the intersection were all associated with an increase in traffic collision counts at the intersections. The years 2018 and 2019 were associated with higher collision counts compared to the reference year, 2015. For the probability component of the model, the existence of traffic signals at the intersection and location along “Main Road”were both associated with an increase in the chances of at least one collision being observed at the intersection, whereas having any high-speed road around the intersection decreased this chance.

publications.title: biclaR: Estimating the Socio-Environmental Impacts of Car Substitution by Bicycle and Public Transit Using Open Tools
publications.abstract: Abstract This paper estimates the potential for cycling combined with public transit (PT) as a substitute for car trips in the Lisbon metropolitan area and assesses its socio-environmental impacts using open data and open source tools. A decision support tool that facilitates the design and development of a metropolitan cycling network was developed ( biclaR ). The social and environmental impacts were assessed using the HEAT for Cycling and the HEAT as a Service tools. The impacts of shifting car trips to PT were also estimated and monetized. The results indicate that 10% of trips could be made by bicycle + PT combination. Shifting to cycling for the first-and-last mile stages can reduce annual CO 2 eq emissions from 3,000 tons/day, with benefits over 10 years of at least €125 million. For the PT leg, the transfer from car avoids up to 20,500 tons of CO 2 eq emissions per year. This evidence can support policymakers to prioritize interventions that reduce the reliance on private motor vehicles.

Engineering in development: transport
publications.venue: White Rose Research Online (University of Leeds, The University of Sheffield, University of York)
publications.abstract: This book is part of a series by Engineers Without Borders UK on technological solutions to the challenge of poverty alleviation. Basic transport infrastructure such as safe roads and bridges are largely taken for granted in the developed world yet silently play a major role in society. In combination with suitable vehicles, this infrastructure boosts mobility, allows access to essential services and, when designed well, enables healthy and sustainable travel for all. These benefits become clear in areas lacking basic transportation technologies. In many areas in low income countries moving food, water and people is difficult and dangerous. Poor quality roads mean that motorised transport further damages critical routes and the local environment, making travel hazardous and unpleasant for other road users. In terms of road accidents and access to medical services, poor transport kills.This book is about how to address some of these issues from an engineering perspective. Transport in Development does not prescribe solutions that attempt to emulate the developed world - where ubiquitous cars have caused entrenched problems of their own. Instead, it takes a pragmatic approach to transport problems, focussing on solutions that can realistically be implemented by a well-organised local community. Based on the 'appropriate technology' ethic, the book provides an overview to solutions - in terms of vehicles and infrastructure - that have been tried and tested.

publications.title: Outdoor lighting and active travel: A high-resolution analysis using satellite imagery and Strava data in Glasgow
publications.abstract: The benefits of active travel are well-established. While previous research has explored how built environment factors (such as population density, accessibility, land use, and infrastructure) influence active travel, micro-scale features like outdoor lighting have received less attention. This study examines associations between outdoor lighting levels and active travel in Glasgow, accounting for broader contextual factors and distinguishing between daylight and dark conditions. We used Strava data, satellite-derived outdoor lighting imagery, and other spatial datasets aggregated to small-area zones in Glasgow. Bayesian spatial models (Besag–York–Mollié) were fitted to estimate associations between contextual variables and distances travelled on foot, by bike, and by both modes combined, separately for daylight and dark hours. Outdoor lighting levels derived from night-time satellite imagery were positively associated with walking, cycling, and overall active-travel distances during both light conditions (daylight and dark). These associations were stronger during dark hours, particularly for cycling. Several contextual relationships also varied by light condition: industrial density was positively associated with cycling only during daylight, while quietness and gradient showed stronger associations during daylight. Population and income deprivation were negatively associated across all modes under both light conditions. Our findings underscore the potential relevance of lighting in shaping active travel patterns after dark, particularly for cycling. They also highlight the need for future research that considers light conditions and time of day in environmental studies of mobility, as well as across broader contexts, specific locations, and diverse population groups – to better inform equitable and effective active travel policy. • Outdoor lighting is positively associated with Strava walking and cycling in Glasgow. • Associations are stronger for cycling, especially during dark hours. • Industrial density, quietness and gradient also show different associations by light condition. • Findings highlight the importance of considering light conditions in active travel research.

publications.title: Spotting rat-runs: A network-based method for identifying potential cut-through routes in Bogotá, Colombia
publications.abstract: Traffic congestion is a growing challenge in many cities. As major corridors become congested, drivers may seek alternative routes through local roads. While this practice, commonly known as ‘rat-running’, reflects an adaptive use of the network to maintain travel efficiency, its concentration in residential areas negatively impacts local populations through reduced road safety, increased pollution, and community severance. Authorities face the complex task of managing these flows to balance overall network efficiency with neighbourhood liveability. However, efforts to assess through-traffic prevalence and target interventions are constrained by limited data, and no systematically established approach currently exists for screening residential networks at city scale. We propose a screening methodology to flag local streets susceptible to cut-through traffic using open data and network analysis. Applying the method to Bogotá, Colombia, we integrated OpenStreetMap road network data, observed speeds on major roads, and traffic offence reports as a proxy for traffic presence. By calculating changes in betweenness centrality (ΔBC) relative to uncongested baseline conditions throughout the day on a travel-time-weighted network graph, we quantified each link's susceptibility to receiving redistributed traffic during congestion. Finally, using a multilevel logistic model, we found that increased ΔBC on residential streets was positively and significantly associated with a higher probability of traffic violation reports. This relationship varied across city sectors, reflecting the influence of local network structure and traffic enforcement intensity. The methodology enables proactive screening independent of historical data. By identifying areas with a high propensity for through-traffic, it supports urban planners and authorities in targeting traffic management interventions, allocating enforcement resources, and informing transport model development.
